verdict: The Italian-specific thinking here is genuinely good in places - the avere-frame paradigm (ho fame / ho freddo), the tu/Lei/voi register split, articles and preposition-fusion promoted to tier 1, the passato prossimo/imperfetto split, ne, ce l'ho, and the correct decision to demote the future - so the spine has clearly been re-thought rather than translated. Three systemic faults undercut it. First, the file is an unmerged two-pass artefact: roughly sixty teachables are duplicated, some at conflicting tiers (caffè hs-0062/hs-0546, mamma hs-0211 t1/hs-0510 t2, papà hs-0120 t1/hs-0509 t2, bagno hs-0169/hs-0564, che ore sono hs-0210 t1/hs-0412 t2, mi può aiutare hs-0197 t1/hs-0476 t2, davanti a three times, sugo three times, buonissimo three times, bancomat, taxi, strada, sopra/sotto/dentro, nessuno, intero, mi manchi, stammi bene, lascia stare, a tavola, mi sono fatto male, ci vediamo, mi fa uno sconto) - the learner will meet the same card twice at different SRS depths, and the later pass also drifts into hyphens where house style calls for en dashes. Second, the notes still narrate the Hindi source to a British learner who has never seen Devanagari: mithai, biryani, garam masala, rickshaws, lakhs, jī, चाय and "so this slot goes to…" all leak through, and each one is a fact the reader cannot use. Third, and most seriously, there is a missing arrival layer that a Hindi spine would never have flagged: no buonasera at all (the greeting for half the waking day), no il bar (the false friend the whole coffee-and-aperitivo culture hangs on), no piazza, mare, ristorante, fermata, museo, tabaccheria, supermercato, coperto or scontrino, no conoscere, uscire or guardare, no secondo me / hai ragione / magari / ti va di…?, no way to say how old you are or to introduce a friend, and - the single biggest hole - not one line of pronunciation teaching (ciao vs che, gelato vs ghiaccio, gn/gli/sci, double consonants, where the stress falls) and no statement that Italian questions are made by intonation alone. For a Latin-script language those look too obvious to teach, which is exactly why they got skipped. Fix the duplicates, strip the Hindi commentary, and add the arrival layer plus a pronunciation and question-formation paradigm, and this becomes a strong 1,100-item Italian course rather than a very well-localised Hindi one.

items.note: Third person of essere. Also 'you are' when using the polite Lei.
'no' answers a question; 'non' goes in front of the verb: non è, non lo so.
Usually left out, since the verb ending already says who: parlo = I speak.
For strangers, shopkeepers, anyone older. Takes third-person verbs: Lei è, Lei parla.
One form for two people: io sono and loro sono.
'Cosa?' alone is what people actually say. 'Che' goes before a noun: che ora è?
Plural is ci sono. C'è un bagno qui? = is there a toilet here?
Changes with the noun: questo, questa, questi, queste.
'That one' is quello / quella.
No apostrophe-s in Italian: la borsa di Anna. Fuses with the article: di + il = del.
In for countries and rooms (in Italia, in cucina), but a for towns: a Roma.
Also marks the person you give or say something to: dico a Marco.
Also 'at someone's place': vado da Marco, da Luigi (the restaurant).
Fuses with the article: sul tavolo, sulla sedia.
No accent: e = and, è = is.
The everyday opener. Allora, andiamo? = right, shall we go?
With friends, family, anyone your age or younger. Italians switch to tu quickly.
Same spelling as sei = six.
Friends only. With strangers say buongiorno (until mid-afternoon) or buonasera.
Shortened to 'vabbè' in fast speech, which leans towards 'yeah, whatever'.
Buono for food and things, bravo for a person who is good at something. The 'oh I see' use of Hindi अच्छा is 'ah, ho capito'.
Anch'io = me too.
Irregular: faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno.
Irregular: vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno.
vengo, vieni, viene, veniamo, venite, vengono.

items.word: parlo / parli / parla / parliamo / parlate / parlano
items.roman: parlo / parli / parla / parliamo / parlate / parlano
items.en: present tense: I speak, you speak, he speaks…
items.note: -are verbs take -o -i -a -iamo -ate -ano; -ere and -ire take -o -i -e -iamo -ete/-ite -ono. This one tense covers 'I speak' and 'I am speaking'.
Keeps its article: il mio telefono, la mia borsa. Dropped for one family member: mia sorella.
Same word as 'his / her', because polite Lei is grammatically third person: il Suo passaporto.
Goes before the verb: mi piace, mi serve, mi dispiace.
Ti va un caffè? The polite version is Le: Le porto il conto.
Dov'è before è.
The same word means 'because', so the answer starts with the question word.
Also 'like, as': come te = like you.
Agrees when counting: quanti anni hai?, quante persone?
Qua is the same thing, used just as much.
Là is the same thing.
Ora means the same but is also the noun 'hour'.
What a waiter says when taking your order. 'Just now, a moment ago' is appena.
Two separate words, and two more beyond them: dopodomani and l'altro ieri.
'Again' is di nuovo.
Tanto is the warmer spoken alternative: grazie tante, mi piace tanto.
Short for un poco; the apostrophe is not optional.
'Too much' is troppo.
'Less' is meno.
Basta così, grazie = that's enough, thanks.
Qualcosa da mangiare = something to eat.
Singular in Italian: la gente è simpatica. 'Persone' is the countable one: tre persone.
Hindi बात ('the thing said') has no single Italian noun. For 'the thing is…' say il fatto è che…
A casa = at home / home (no preposition faff).
Italians mostly say 'mi chiamo' rather than using this noun.
In a bar you specify: naturale (still) or frizzante (sparkling).
The social offer drink in Italy, and un caffè always means an espresso. Tea exists - un tè caldo, un tè freddo in summer - but nobody drinks it with milk.
'Food' is il cibo, but people say 'qualcosa da mangiare'.
Always plural. Denaro is the formal one.
Also means 'weather'. Clock time is ora, and 'a time, an occasion' is volta.
Same word as 'what?'. Una cosa = a thing.
Also 'a spot on the train': è libero questo posto?
do, dai, dà, diamo, date, danno.
Prendo un caffè, prendo il treno. The workhorse of ordering.
Guardare = to watch, to look at.
Ascoltare = to listen to on purpose.
dico, dici, dice, diciamo, dite, dicono.
For arranging to meet, Italians say vedersi: ci vediamo alle otto. For meeting someone new it's conoscere: ho conosciuto Anna ieri. Incontrare leans towards 'run into'.
Conoscere is for knowing a person or a place. so, sai, sa, sappiamo, sapete, sanno.
Hindi पता also means 'known'; that sense is sapere in Italian (hs-0187).
Adds -isc-: capisco, capisci, capisce, capiamo, capite, capiscono.
Come stai? uses this, not essere. Living somewhere is abitare or vivere.
voglio, vuoi, vuole… Say vorrei (I'd like) when asking for things; 'voglio' sounds blunt.
bevo, bevi, beve, beviamo, bevete, bevono.
'Let's walk there' is andiamo a piedi.
Ti preparo un caffè. For most 'make' senses fare does the job.
Also 'to put on' clothes: mi metto il cappotto.

items.en: commands: tu form vs polite Lei form
items.note: They swap endings: -are gives parla (tu) / parli (Lei); -ere and -ire give senti (tu) / senta (Lei). Hence scusa to a friend, scusi to a stranger.
Any 'we' form works as 'let's': facciamo, prendiamo. 'Dai!' adds the nudge.
Pure softens an invitation to 'go ahead and…'. Polite: entri pure.

items.en: please sit down, make yourself at home
items.note: Said constantly by hosts, waiters and receptionists. To a friend: accomodati.
Handing something over. Ecco on its own = there it is.
What a shopkeeper says when it's your turn. To a friend: dimmi.
To a friend: scusa. Use it to stop a stranger in the street.
For sympathy or regret. Scusa is for apologising for something you did.
Per piacere and per cortesia are the same thing.

items.en: you're welcome; after you; go ahead
items.note: The all-purpose reply to grazie. 'Don't mention it' is di niente or figurati.
To a friend: come stai?
Stare, not essere. 'Sono bene' is wrong.
Literally 'I call myself'. 'Sono Antoine' works too.
To a friend: come ti chiami?
You 'have' hunger in Italian, you are not it.
Dovere = must: devo, devi, deve.
Also opens a sentence for effect: ma dai! = come off it!
Oppure for a fuller 'or else'.
Identical to 'why?'. Perché non vieni? Perché lavoro.
For surprise Italians say 'ma dai!' or 'oh!'.
Also the indefinite article: un caffè, una birra, uno zaino (before s+consonant or z), un'amica.
Same word as 'you are'.
Don't mix up with nuovo = new.
The neutral word; in conversation people say mamma (hs-0211).
Stress the end: papà. Padre is the formal 'father'.
Plural fratelli also covers 'brothers and sisters'.
Affectionate address to a child is tesoro or amore, not this.
Italian mums and nonne do ask this out of care, but it isn't a greeting. The greeting slot is come va? or tutto bene?
Piano means slowly here, not quietly-only. To a friend: parla più piano.
A raised 'Come?' does the same job in one word.
Also used as a plain 'right, I see' in conversation.

items.en: how do you say this in Italian?
items.note: Come si dice ... = how do you say ...
Lower case. No article after parlare: parlo italiano. But studio l'italiano, and l'italiano è bello.
Also 'in order to' before an infinitive: per mangiare.
Con me, con te (not 'con mi').
ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno; the h is silent. Avere is also the auxiliary for the everyday past: ho mangiato, ho visto.
posso, puoi, può… Posso? on its own = may I?
A presto! = see you soon. 'Fast' is veloce, 'in a rush' is di fretta.
Italian has no word for o'clock: sono le tre, alle otto. One o'clock is the singular: è l'una, all'una.
Amica for a woman; plural amici / amiche.
How you address any woman you don't know. Close family friends may be called zia (auntie), just like Hindi aunty.
Drops the -e before a surname: signor Rossi.
Il mio ragazzo also means 'my boyfriend'.
Odd plural: uomini.
Ci porta il conto? = could you bring us the bill?
Aperto = open (the sign on the door).
Chiuso = closed, which you will read a lot at 1pm.
A mobile is il cellulare or il telefonino.
Never used face to face. Literally 'ready'.
Ti chiamo dopo = I'll ring you later.
Two chats: parlare con qualcuno is to talk to someone; fare due chiacchiere is to have a natter.
The everyday staple. Pasta is a course in its own right (il primo), never a side dish, and rice is riso.
Hindi dal has no Italian twin; sugo is the everyday thing that goes on the staple. Salsa is a cold or bottled sauce.
Usually singular: mangio verdura. Contorno = the veg side dish on a menu.
Ordering 'a latte' in Italy gets you a glass of milk. Say caffellatte.
Comes up far less than in India; mostly for arrabbiata or nduja.
Fare colazione = to have breakfast, usually standing at the bar with a coffee and a cornetto.
What the host says. Ne = 'of it', and Italians never drop it.
Add complimenti! to praise the cook. -issimo is the everyday intensifier.
Again 'I have thirst', like ho fame.
The everyday word; auto is also fine, automobile is stiff. Macchina also means machine.
Stanza is any room in a house.
Asking for il bagno in a bar is normal and expected.
Never changes: dieci euro, not 'euri'.
Plural things: quanto costano? For a total: quant'è?
To a friend: aspetta!
One form for both genders; plural grandi.
Magari means 'maybe' too, but also 'I wish!' as an answer.
Literally 'it pleases me', so the thing you like is the subject.
Softens a request or holds someone off: scusi, un attimo.
In Italia = in / to Italy.
Language and nationality, lower case: sono inglese.
Very spoken. Luggage is i bagagli.

items.word: sono / sei / è / siamo / siete / sono
items.roman: sono / sei / e / siamo / siete / sono
items.note: io and loro share 'sono'. Alongside it learn ho / hai / ha / abbiamo / avete / hanno (to have), which Italian uses for age, hunger and thirst.
Adverb. The adjective is buono.
Said at the start of every meal; the reply is grazie, altrettanto. 'Help yourself' is serviti pure.
The polite way to ask for anything. For 'I need' say mi serve ...
Il mio piatto preferito = my favourite dish.
The 'lo' is compulsory; bare 'so' isn't said.
A shrugged 'boh' is the everyday shorthand.
To a younger person: parli inglese?
To a friend: di dove sei? The 'di' is not optional.
Also scozzese, gallese, irlandese, britannico. Or vengo dall'Inghilterra.
Plural: dove sono ...?
On the phone: pronto, sono Antoine.
On the phone: resti in linea = hold the line.
In an emergency just shout aiuto!
The polite goodbye; ciao is for friends. ArrivederLa is extra formal.
Warm and informal, at the end of a call or a visit.
The Italian version of offering tea. Refusing twice is normal; so is being overruled.
Bambina for a girl, bambini for children in general.
Patatine = crisps or chips.

items.en: the two levels of 'you', plus the plural
items.note: tu with friends and family; Lei with strangers, and it takes third-person verbs (Lei parla). Voi is 'you lot' for everyone, formal or not. Italians offer 'diamoci del tu' when it's time to relax.
Also grazie tante, or a warm grazie infinite.
Pointing at something on a menu or a market stall.
Un'altra volta = one more time. Ancora also works.
Tagged onto the end of a statement. Vero? is the same. Italian has no do-you-don't-you juggling.
The productive way to adjust a dish: senza aglio, senza glutine, senza formaggio. 'Not too spicy' is non troppo piccante.
Answer: sono le due, è l'una.
What everyone actually says, at any age.

items.en: titles used as a mark of respect
items.note: Where Hindi adds जी after a name, Italian puts a title before the surname. Dottore for any graduate, professore for a teacher, and they get used far more than in Britain.
Only ever heard in ho fame, che fame!
Non ce l'ho = I haven't got it. The 'ce' is filler you just have to keep.
Plural: non ci sono.
Quello lì = that one. Pointing in a shop.
Opens a sentence to a friend. Polite version: senta.
Never dropped as in English: penso che sia tardi, not 'penso sia tardi' in speech.
Softens or nudges: vieni, dai! Ma dai! = you're joking.

items.en: right now: I'm speaking, you're doing
items.note: stare + -ando (-are) or -endo (-ere/-ire). Only for what's happening at this second; for everything else the plain present does the job, unlike English.

items.word: ero / eri / era / eravamo / eravate / erano
items.roman: ero / eri / era / eravamo / eravate / erano
items.note: The imperfect of essere, for describing the past. C'era = there was, c'erano = there were.
Agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: sua madre could be his mother or hers.
Il nostro, la nostra.
Com'è la pizza? For people: com'è fatto? or che tipo è?
Qual è (no apostrophe) = which is.
Giornata is the day as a stretch of time: buona giornata!

items.en: to tell, to fill someone in
items.note: Raccontami tutto! For 'tell me' in the sense of 'go on', Italians use dimmi.
Chiedere = to ask for something; domandare is rarer in speech.
Mi sembra strano = it seems odd to me. 'It takes an hour' is ci vuole un'ora.
Reflexive: mi siedo, siediti! Italians more often say accomodarsi (hs-0087).
Reflexive: mi alzo alle sette.
A tu command turns into the plain infinitive when negated: parla! but non parlare! The Lei form just adds non: non parli.
Standard over a bar counter: mi dà un caffè? To a friend: mi dai ...?
For a waiter or someone at a desk. To a friend: senti, scusa.
Formal only, in an office or a letter. Grazie covers everything else.
Reply: tutto bene, grazie. Also tutto a posto?
Reply: va bene, or non c'è male.
Mi piace la pizza but mi piacciono gli spaghetti. The verb follows the thing liked.
Don't confuse with sé (himself) or six, sei.
Extremely common filler. 'What does it mean?' is che vuol dire?
Adds punch: è proprio buono = it really is good.

items.en: adjectives agree in gender and number
items.note: Every noun is masculine or feminine and the adjective follows: un caffè freddo, una birra fredda. Adjectives in -e have only two forms: grande / grandi. Most adjectives go after the noun.
Also a presto, a domani, a dopo.
Said to someone who is unwell or off travelling. Formal: si riguardi.
Fino a domani, fino alla stazione.

items.en: the everyday past: I spoke, I went
items.note: avere + past participle for most verbs, but essere for verbs of coming and going (andare, venire, uscire, stare, nascere) and all reflexives. With essere the ending agrees: sono andata, siamo andati. This is the past tense Italians actually speak.
Re-tiered down: in speech Italians use the present plus a time word (domani vado a Roma). The real future is mostly for predictions and promises.

items.word: il / lo / la / i / gli / le (a + il = al, di + la = della)
items.roman: il / lo / la / i / gli / le
items.en: 'the', and how it fuses with prepositions
items.note: Re-tiered to tier 1: nothing works without it. il before most masculine nouns, lo before s+consonant, z, ps and gn (lo zaino), l' before a vowel, la feminine; plurals i / gli / le. Then a+il=al, di+il=del, in+il=nel, da+la=dalla, su+le=sulle. Italian also uses 'the' where English drops it: mi piace il caffè.
Italian does this with plain verbs, not a special mood: Posso? = may I? Ti va di …? = do you fancy …? The 'we' form alone proposes: andiamo? facciamo così?
Quello con il formaggio. Job words take suffixes instead: barista, giornalaio, fornaio.
Più di before nouns and numbers; più che when comparing two adjectives or verbs.
Il ristorante più buono della città. Article, noun, then più.
È successo = it happened. È andata bene = it went well.
Penso di sì / penso di no = I think so / I don't think so. Careful speech puts a subjunctive after che, but plenty of people don't.
Dovrei is the softened 'ought to'; devo is a flat 'I have to'.
'Some' is di + article: dell'acqua, del pane, delle patatine.
A dopo! = see you later.
Prima di cena, prima di partire.
A volte = sometimes.
Needs the double negative: non ci vado mai.
Ogni giorno means the same.
Always followed by a singular: ogni volta, ogni persona.
Un altro caffè = another coffee. Altro? = anything else?
Non ho niente. On its own it also means 'no worries'.
È tutto? = is that everything? (at a till).
Un'ora, due ore. Also means 'now'.
Age uses avere: ho quarant'anni.
Di mattina = in the mornings. Stamattina = this morning.
Buonasera starts surprisingly early, from about 4pm.
Buonanotte is only said when someone is off to bed.
L'altro ieri = the day before yesterday. Italian keeps them apart, unlike Hindi परसों.
Never changes: duecento, trecento.
Plural is irregular: duemila, tremila.
Time: le due e mezza. Mezz'ora = half an hour.
On a menu il primo is the pasta course, il secondo the meat or fish.
Plural mogli.
Re-tiered down: in-laws come up far less in Italian small talk than in Hindi.
I suoceri = the in-laws.
Just the word, not a form of address, unlike Hindi भाभी. Cognato for a brother-in-law.
False friend: parenti are relatives; parents are i genitori.
I figli when you mean your own children of any age.
Sposato / sposata = married.
Pensare a = to think about, pensare di = to have an opinion on.
Studiare = to study.
Fare la spesa = to do the food shopping; fare shopping is clothes.
Scrivimi! = text me.
Mandare un messaggio = to text. Inviare is formal.
Uscire = to go out of a place, and also to go out for the evening.
Takes essere in the past: sono arrivato.
Also to taste and to try on. Cercare di = to try to do something.
Iniziare is the same thing.
È finito il pane = we've run out of bread.
Mi sono dimenticato is just as common.
Prende male = the signal's bad.
Formal: La richiamo dopo.
Back to front from English: the person missed is the subject, so 'mi manchi' is literally 'you are lacking to me'.
Il dolce as a noun is the pudding course.
Mal di pancia = tummy ache. Stomaco is the clinical word.
A bit blunt; 'sono a posto così' is the softer refusal a host will accept.
Stamp regional tickets before boarding: convalidare.
Also just 'il bus'. A long-distance coach is il pullman.
No rickshaws in Italy; the taxi fills that short-hop slot. You ring for one or find a rank, you don't hail it.
Also a greetings card.
Via in addresses: via Roma. Per strada = out in the street.
Sempre dritto = keep going straight on. Also spelled diritto.
Also 'dear' at the start of a letter, and a term of affection.
In speech: costa poco. 'A buon mercato' is a good bargain.
For people, anziano is the polite word.
Ho caldo = I'm hot; fa caldo = the weather is hot.
Ho freddo, fa freddo.
Non funziona = it isn't working. 'Bad' is cattivo or brutto.
Giusto! as a reply = quite right.
Felice is the deeper, weightier one.
Sporco = dirty.
Same word as the phone 'hello'. Pronti? Via! = ready, steady, go.
'Necessary' in speech is more often serve: mi serve il passaporto.
The warm way to accept an invitation, and the polite way to say yes to another coffee.
Assolutamente on its own is ambiguous and best avoided.
Sul serio? and ma dai! do the same job.
Abbastanza bene = pretty well, a safe answer to come stai?
Così tanto = this much. Va bene così = that's fine as it is.
Also means 'alone': sono solo.
Che + adjective is the all-purpose exclamation: che buono! che caldo!
Also non preoccuparti. Formal: non si preoccupi.
A woman says divertita. Shorter: è stato bellissimo.
Plural things: ti sono piaciuti?
Auguri! is for birthdays and best wishes.

items.en: ciao bella! / ciao bello! (warm, informal address)
items.note: Ciao bella to a woman friend is warm, not a chat-up line. Man to man it reads as teasing or flirty, so stick to ciao + the name, or ragazzi for a group.
Also 'bless you' after a sneeze, and 'cheers' with a glass.
Formal: come si sente?
Also how Italians address anyone with a degree. The medical one is il medico.
La farmacia is the chemist's, and pharmacists give a lot of front-line advice.
Mi fa male la testa = my head hurts. Ho mal di gola = I've got a sore throat.
Riposati! = get some rest.
Same word as 'time'. Che tempo fa? = what's the weather like?
Feminine despite the -e. Fa caldo = it's hot.
Fa freddo = it's cold. A head cold is il raffreddore.
Piove = it's raining.
Never changes in the plural: le città. In centro = in the town centre.
Un paesino in Toscana. Plain paese covers both village and country.
Also means a village, so context does the work.
In vacanza = on holiday. Le ferie is time off work; a day off is un giorno libero.
Feminine and unchanging: la foto, le foto.
Un vestito on its own is a dress or a suit.
Re-tiered up: with friends this is the one you use daily. Il tuo, la tua.
Never changes shape, but keeps the article: il loro cane, la loro casa.
Vi porto il conto = I'll bring you the bill. The formal singular is Le.
In everyday speech gli also does duty for 'to them'.
Same word as the question: quando arrivo, ti chiamo.
Perciò means the same. Allora is the more casual one.
Andiamo fuori a cena = let's eat out.
Di sopra = upstairs.
Di sotto = downstairs.
Di fronte a is the same. Handy for meeting points: davanti al bar.
È lontano? = is it far? Vicino = near.
Italian does not split grandparents by side as Hindi does; i nonni covers both couples, and you add materni or paterni only if it matters.
The same word means host, so context decides. Sei mio ospite = it's on me.

items.en: pastries (what you take to someone's house)
items.note: The Italian equivalent of turning up with mithai: a tray of paste from the pasticceria, tied with ribbon.
La frutta is the whole category; un frutto is one piece.
Mango has no cultural twin in Italy; mela, arancia and pesca are the everyday fruits.
The flavour base Italians actually talk about, where Hindi has मसाला. Spices are le spezie, but they come up far less.
Un bicchiere di vino. The material glass is il vetro.
Also means cooking and cuisine: la cucina italiana.
Sono vegetariano / vegetariana. Expect to be asked whether fish counts.
feminine despite the -o: la mano, le mani. Arm = il braccio (plural le braccia).
Leg = la gamba; a piedi = on foot.
A woman says sono stanca. Sono stanco morto = shattered.
The whole ritual: piacere, and you shake hands. Piacere di conoscerti is the fuller version.
Spoken Italian prefers this to mostrare: mi fa vedere quello? = can you show me that one?
lavarsi = to wash yourself; lavare i piatti = do the washing-up.
Also lascia perdere, same job.
Said ti-vu. La televisione in full.
Everyone's default; the verb is scrivere su WhatsApp.
Ti mando un messaggio = I'll text you.
Everyday Italian usually says tutto il/la: tutto il giorno = the whole day.
Needs the double negative: non c'e nessuno = there's nobody there.
fai cosi = do it like this; e cosi = that's how it is.

items.en: can you give me a discount?
items.note: Haggling only really works at markets in Italy, not in shops.
il finestrino for a car, train or plane window.
Feminine: le chiavi.
dai, andiamo! Dai is the all-purpose 'come on'.

items.word: ho fame / ho freddo / ho mal di testa
items.roman: ho fame / ho freddo / ho mal di testa
items.en: 'I have [state]' frame: Italian uses avere, not essere, for bodily states
items.note: ho fame, sete, sonno, freddo, caldo, paura, ragione, mal di testa. Saying sono freddo means you're a cold person.
perfetto and benissimo do the same job in conversation.

items.en: how much does it come to?
items.note: At the till. Quanto le devo? is the politer version.
Formal, for a taxi driver. To a friend: fermati qui.
piu avanti = further on; avanti! = come in!
vicino a = near to: vicino alla stazione.

items.en: noun and adjective plurals: libro/libri, casa/case, chiave/chiavi
items.note: Gender and number drive the article and the adjective too: la casa bianca, le case bianche.
Formal: entri pure / venga. Pure here means 'go ahead and'.
Formal: che lavoro fa?
Abitare, not vivere, for 'live somewhere'.
a with towns, in with countries: abito in Inghilterra.
Weather uses fare: fa caldo, fa freddo.

items.en: that works for me, fine by me

items.note: davvero? = really?; e vero = it's true.
The standard goodbye between friends: ci vediamo domani.
la memoria = the faculty; un ricordo = a particular memory.
Italian just uses di. Riguardo a / a proposito di are heavier and more formal.
parla piu piano = speak more slowly. Lentamente is the textbook word.
e libero questo posto? = is this seat free? il sedile is the seat of a car.

items.word: a che ora parte il treno?
items.roman: a che ora parte il treno?
items.en: what time does the train leave?

items.note: Il treno e in ritardo. Tardi is 'late' in time-of-day terms: e tardi.
Expect chiuso in the early afternoon and on Mondays.
un etto = 100g, the unit you'll actually use at the deli counter.
Ordering frame: mi da un chilo di pomodori?
Small bars often can't change a 50 euro note.
Worth asking: plenty of small places still prefer cash.
Also fare da mangiare = to make some food.
What staff say to you. Between friends it's dimmi.
fermati! = stop! Il treno si ferma a Pisa.
e finito il pane = we've run out of bread.
ho perso il portafoglio / il treno.
ci facciamo una videochiamata?
The mal di + body part pattern: mal di gola, mal di pancia, mal di schiena.
mal di stomaco is the higher-up ache; pancia is the everyday word.
una volta = once; due volte = twice; la prossima volta.
A taxi fare is la corsa; a ticket price is il biglietto.
la via in addresses: via Roma.
Worth checking before you book anything in August.
lavare i piatti. Le stoviglie is the formal cover word.
The everyday fresh cheese. Il formaggio = cheese in general, il parmigiano for grating.
Odd plural: le uova, feminine.
Spoken Italian prefers the reflexive: mi sono dimenticato.
ancora un po' = a bit more.
se piove, resto a casa. Allora is often left out.

items.word: con me / per te / da lui
items.roman: con me / per te / da lui
items.en: after a preposition Italian uses the stressed forms me, te, lui, lei, noi, voi, loro
items.note: Never con io / per tu. da me also means 'at my place'.
No special construction for possession: ho una macchina, ho due fratelli.
sei mai stato a Roma? = have you ever been? non ci sono mai stato = I've never been.
posso entrare? posso vedere? The single most useful frame for a traveller.
Plural: quanto costano?
che stai facendo? = what are you doing right this second?
The polite way to stop a host refilling your plate or glass.
aiuto! on its own = help!
cosa significa? is the fuller, more formal version.
di chi e questo? = whose is this?
cos'e successo? = what happened? diventare = to become.
For a passing bug people say non sto bene rather than sono malato.
Softer, warmer version of un po'.
sopra il tavolo; su also does this job.
di fronte a = directly facing.
Opposite fuori = outside.
From 17 the pattern flips: dici- goes first.
One o'clock is the only singular: e l'una.
Everything from two on takes sono le…, feminine (le ore is understood).
Minutes are simply added: le quattro e venti, le cinque meno dieci.
stasera = this evening; di mattina, di pomeriggio, di notte follow the same pattern.
What you call him and what you call him to others: mio papa. Il padre is neutral-formal.
La madre is the formal word; nobody says it at home.
hai fratelli? covers brothers and sisters together.
In speech: mio fratello piu grande.
In speech: mia sorella piu piccola.

items.en: birth order is optional in Italian: add piu grande / piu piccolo (formally maggiore / minore) only if it matters
items.note: Unlike Hindi, no kin term is marked for age on its own.
No special address form: you call her by her first name.
Again, first names only; i suoceri = the in-laws.

items.en: excuse me! (to a man or woman you don't know)
items.note: This is how you flag down a stranger. Signore / signora only really appear in staff-to-customer speech.
No extra word needed for 'you all'. Calling out to a group of friends: ragazzi!
ciao a tutti = hi everyone.
The warm yes. Also eh si and certo che si.
Standard warmth in any catch-up.
Mutton isn't really eaten; lamb is the festive meat, especially at Easter.
Feminine despite the -e.
The northern cooking fat; olive oil does the job everywhere else.
olio d'oliva, on the table at nearly every meal.
Sliced loaf = pane in cassetta; a bread roll = un panino.
pranzare = to have lunch; the main meal, roughly 1pm.
Eaten late, from 8pm. cenare = to have dinner.
The everyday flatbread snack; la piadina in Emilia-Romagna.
The northern rice primo: alla milanese, ai funghi, ai frutti di mare. Made to order, so it takes twenty minutes.
The standard fried street snack; il suppli in Rome, arancina (f) in Palermo.
Also sott'olio for oil-preserved veg on an antipasto plate.
The sauce that goes on everything. La salsa is any other sauce.
Breakfast is coffee and biscotti far more often than anything cooked.
Don't confuse with il peperone = pepper (capsicum).
un caffe means an espresso. A caffe latte is a milky drink; ordering 'a latte' gets you a glass of milk.
che buono! is the compliment you pay a cook. Buono covers 'tasty'.
Vegetarianism is the marked category in Italy; there's no word for 'non-veg'. senza carne = without meat.
ho sete = I'm thirsty.
versare = to pour a drink; aggiungere = to add.
scaldo l'acqua; riscaldare for reheating leftovers.
The ne can't be dropped: it stands in for 'of it'.

items.en: shall I make you a coffee?
items.note: The standard offer the moment anyone walks in.

items.en: dinner's ready, come and sit down
items.note: e pronto! does the same job.
Casual: che si mangia stasera?
Watch the false friend: caldo = hot, not cold.
Lunchtime staple; also menu del giorno.
primo piatto = pasta/rice course, secondo = meat or fish.
la scodella for soup.
la tazzina = the little espresso cup; il bicchiere = glass.
il cucchiaino = teaspoon; la forchetta, il coltello complete the set.
la cucina italiana = Italian cooking, same word.
dov'e il bagno? Asking for la toilette works but bagno is what people say.
camera da letto = bedroom; a letto = in bed.
la tavola when it's laid for a meal: a tavola!
avete un tavolo per due? on arriving at a restaurant.
fare il bagno = to have a bath, or to swim in the sea.
In the house people just say la luce.
accendi la luce; e andata via la luce = the power's gone.
Short for frigorifero; nobody says the long form.
Also 'to light': accendere una candela.
togliere = to remove or take off.
In an Italian summer you're more likely to say accendi l'aria.

items.en: tu-imperative with the pronoun stuck on the end: dammi (give me), fallo (do it), chiudila (shut it)
items.note: da', fa', di', va', sta' double the following consonant: dimmi, fammi, dammi. This is the everyday household request.

items.en: 'do it for yourself' colouring: mangiati un panino, prenditi un caffe, fatti una doccia
items.note: An extra reflexive pronoun that adds warmth and 'go on, treat yourself'. Optional but very Italian.
Plural gli occhi.
in bocca al lupo = good luck; answer crepi!
ho sonno = I'm sleepy. Il sogno = dream, don't mix them up.
ho freddo = I'm cold; fa freddo = it's cold out.
mi fa male la schiena = my back hurts.
Italian pharmacists give advice over the counter; la farmacia is the first stop.
Never changes: due macchine blu. azzurro = sky blue, the football-team blue.
a chi lo dici! = tell me about it.
di dove sei? is how you ask where someone's from.
con me, per me, da me, secondo me. Not io in these slots.
Also 'in my view': per me e troppo caro.
vieni con me.
The polite you is Lei, third person and often capitalised.
The ce is obligatory when 'have' means 'have on you': ce l'ho, non ce l'ho.
adesso and ora are interchangeable.
Also the universal filler that starts a sentence: allora, senti…
e poi = and then. dopo = after(wards).
Spoken only: non e mica caro = it's not that expensive. Mica male! = not bad at all!
Negative tu commands use the infinitive: non fare, non preoccuparti, non ti preoccupare.
Entrambi is bookish; tutti e due is what people say.
proprio bello = really lovely; proprio non lo so = I really don't know.

items.en: to take, to bring, to carry
items.note: portare via = to take away; da portare via = takeaway.
Also of machines: non funziona is 'it doesn't work' for objects.
Backwards from English: the thing does the liking. mi e piaciuta la citta.
Present tense covers the near future in Italian.
For shopping: dove posso comprare…?
The local short-hop vehicle. You hire one rather than flag one down, and a helmet is compulsory.
To a taxi driver: mi porta alla stazione?

items.en: how much will it come to?
items.note: Italian taxis run on the meter, so you check e a tassametro? rather than haggling the fare.
caro also means 'dear' as in beloved.
Or mi fa vedere quello? pointing at it.
What the person behind the counter asks. Fuller: desidera altro?
Closes an order at the deli or bar.
sicuro? = you sure? di sicuro = definitely.
ti chiamo = I'll call you; una chiamata persa = a missed call.
ho il telefono scarico = my phone's dead; il caricabatterie = charger.
Standard on the phone after pronto?
mi vedi? on a video call.
il tempo = both weather and time.
The standard way to open or change a topic. guarda… works too; formal: senta.

items.en: past tense (passato prossimo): most verbs take avere, verbs of movement and change take essere
items.note: With essere the ending agrees: sono andata, siamo andati. This is the everyday past, the simple past is literary.

items.en: leave it to me, I'll sort it
items.note: The reassuring reply to any small problem.
forse is the plain 'maybe'.
Often vediamo un po'.
Also when a lot of shops shut, roughly 1pm to 4pm.
di questi tempi is the grumblier version.
No word for their house; you'd just say a casa dei suoceri.
aspetta! or un attimo! = hang on a second.
Reflexive: ricordarsi di qualcosa.

items.en: so, tell me all about it
items.note: The staple opener once the small talk is done. Also che mi racconti?
hotel is used just as much. For eating out: trattoria and osteria are the everyday places.
gira a destra = turn right.
ho sbagliato = I got it wrong / my mistake.
Does far more work than English 'beautiful': un bel film, che bella giornata.
a proposito… = by the way, when you're introducing something new.
Mildly slangy but very common with friends. Neutral versions: che bello! and mitico!
ci ha detto tutto = he told us everything. ci also means 'there': ci vado domani.
Spoken Italian uses gli for 'to them' too; loro in that slot is formal and written.

items.en: used to do / was doing: -avo, -evo, -ivo endings
items.note: Covers habits, descriptions and background: da piccolo andavo sempre al mare.

items.en: was in the middle of doing (stare + gerund, past)
items.note: Only for 'right at that moment'; the plain imperfetto usually does the job.

items.en: have done / did: avere or essere + past participle
items.note: Regular participles: -ato, -uto, -ito. Learn fatto, detto, preso, visto, letto as irregulars early.

items.en: pronominal verbs: a stuck-on pronoun changes the meaning (me ne vado = I'm off, non ce la faccio = I can't manage)
items.note: Very frequent in speech and unguessable from the base verb.

items.en: having done X: dopo aver + past participle
items.note: Casual speech often just uses e poi: ho mangiato e poi sono uscito.
mi tocca lavorare domenica. Dovere is the plain 'have to'.
One word covers all of them: il libro che ho letto, la ragazza che parla. cui after a preposition: la casa in cui abito.
l'ho fatto da solo. io stesso = I myself, emphatic.
non ancora = not yet; ancora un po' = a bit more.
vado lo stesso = I'll go anyway.
Days are lower case and mostly masculine, except la domenica.
No single word for it, unlike Hindi: un'ora e mezza, un chilo e mezzo.
Goes after the number: dieci minuti circa. quasi = almost.
Comes after the noun: la settimana prossima.
l'anno scorso, la settimana scorsa.
faccio tardi = I'll be late. Ten minutes late is not late in Italy.
c'e un bar qui vicino?
qui and qua are interchangeable: vieni qua.
li and la likewise interchangeable.
One word for every uncle, and zii for aunt-and-uncle together.
Often shortened to il vicino.
The default celebration wish, birthdays, name days, Christmas. Auguri! on its own is enough.
One word for all three: e festa oggi = it's a holiday today.
The day Italy shuts down and everyone goes to the coast. Natale and Pasqua are the family festivals.
andare a messa. Church-going is far more occasional than the Hindi original assumes.
Both senses: pane fresco, and fa fresco stasera = it's cool this evening.
ho il raffreddore. Nothing to do with freddo the temperature.
Masculine. il pronto soccorso = A&E.
e arrabbiato con me. Also the sauce: penne all'arrabbiata.
ti voglio bene for family and friends; ti amo only for a partner.
Constantly used. meno male che sei arrivato.
fare un giro = to go for a wander; girare per Roma.
suonare for an instrument: suono la chitarra.
accompagnare = to drop someone off; partire = to leave (depart).
non risponde = he's not picking up.
chiamare = to call someone over; ti invito a cena.
me lo spieghi? = can you explain it to me?
ci metto un'ora = it takes me an hour; quanto ci metti?
mi metto la giacca. portare or indossare = to be wearing.
scendo alla prossima = I'm getting off at the next stop. salire = to get on.
No preposition: cerco la stazione.
The standard phone sign-off; ci vediamo is for meeting in person.
Invariable: due film.
The national obsession and a reliable conversation opener: per chi tifi?
il telegiornale (il tg) = the TV news.
Doubling for gradualness, as in Hindi: piano piano si impara.
attento! shouted on its own = watch out!
Before a noun in the plural it means 'several': diverse persone.
e libero questo posto? vuoto = empty.
Signals you're wrapping up a conversation.
Softer spoken version: guarda, e che…
In speech people just say fai cosi.
non ho spiccioli. Also la moneta for coins collectively.
Typical when the kettle and the hob go on together in a holiday flat.
c'e il sole = it's sunny; al sole = in the sun.
l'aria = air; c'e vento = it's windy.
You book one or find a rank, hailing on the street rarely works.
vorrei is the polite form you'll use all day in shops and bars; voglio can sound blunt.
le sette e mezza. e un quarto / meno un quarto for the quarters.
The safe middle ground when ciao feels too familiar and buongiorno too stiff.
Never sono freddo, that says you're a cold fish.
con mezz'ora di ritardo.
c'era traffico is the standard excuse.
scusi, scendo! to get through a crowded bus.
The text you send on landing; a woman writes arrivata.
Italian counts tracks, not platforms: binario 7.
orario continuato = open all day, no lunchtime closing.
il conto, per favore. It won't arrive until you ask.
la pillola too; compressa is what's printed on the box.
Feminine: ho la tosse.
al giorno / alla settimana for 'per day, per week'.

items.en: 21 to 99: decade + unit written as one word
items.note: The decade drops its final vowel before uno and otto: ventuno, ventotto, trentuno. Tre takes an accent when it ends a number: ventitré, trentatré.
No paired 'then' word needed: quando arrivi, chiamami.

items.en: comparative and superlative: piu caro di, il piu caro
items.note: Irregulars worth knowing: buono/migliore/meglio, cattivo/peggiore/peggio.
Again, no dedicated word as in Hindi.
meno un quarto = quarter to.
A brand name that became the word for both the machine and the card.
ho una prenotazione a nome…; prenotare = to book.
la via = street; il viale = avenue.
In speech: c'e un sacco di gente.
i carabinieri are the other force; 112 for emergencies.
Italy has no everyday traditional dress, so this slot holds the ordinary garment word.
la camicia = shirt with a collar; il maglione = jumper.
Ordinary Italian, just a weaker custom: many Italian homes now do ask, and a host will often hand you le ciabatte. Not something the language lacks.
buone feste covers the whole season; buona Pasqua at Easter.
Warm sign-off to someone you're fond of.
A woman says mi sono fatta male.
In speech: ho la nausea, ho vomitato.
sono allergico ai frutti di mare, worth having ready in restaurants.
ho la pressione alta.
Masculine despite the -e: sono diabetico.
la carta in smarter restaurants; il menu is universal.

items.en: could you wrap it up for me?
items.note: For food to take away say 'da portare via'

items.en: send it to me on WhatsApp
items.note: WhatsApp is the default channel in Italy; formal: me lo manda su WhatsApp?
Asking a stranger: mi fa una foto?

items.word: mi si è scaricato il telefono
items.roman: mi si e scaricato il telefono
items.note: è scarico = it's flat

items.word: qual è la password del wifi?
items.roman: qual e la password del wifi?

items.note: Mild; mamma mia covers the surprised or exasperated version

items.en: do come and see us again
items.note: Standard host's goodbye; formal torni a trovarci
Agrees: da sola, da soli
scusi (formal) vs scusa (to a friend)
Also 'their' after a noun; Loro as a formal 'you' is dead - use voi
tornare indietro = to go back
Imperfect of avere/essere + participle; far rarer in speech than the Hindi equivalent
Same form does 'we go' and 'let's go'
mi servono with plurals; ho bisogno di … is the fuller form
Also rimettiti presto
buon viaggio! is the send-off
Also 'paper'; posso pagare con la carta?
è la prima volta che vengo qui
dietro alla chiesa; the 'a' is often dropped in speech
fuori alone = out, outside
Takes a bare infinitive: senza pagare
Same word as 'how'; è come il tè inglese
per colpa di when it's someone's fault
Standard reply to come stai?; also insomma
You answer the phone with pronto
il volume for the sound level
parla più forte = speak up
mi sono divertito = I had a great time
all'inizio = at first
non ho voglia = I don't feel like it - the everyday way to decline
venti drops its -i before uno and otto: ventuno, ventotto
il terzo piano = the third floor
Italian has no formal/casual split for 'time': tempo = time in general, ora = clock time, orario = opening hours and schedules
One o'clock is singular: è l'una
From two onwards: sono le due
tra (or fra) + a period = in X time
Timetables and formal speech use the 24-hour clock: le ventidue
Literally 'how many of them do we have'; che giorno è oggi? asks the day
Lower case and no 'on': lunedì vado a Roma
Italian has a single word for Sunday - no formal/colloquial pair as in Hindi. il lunedì with the article = on Mondays
sono sposato / sposata; conviviamo = we live together
One word for every aunt; gli zii = aunt and uncle together
Plural cugini covers a mixed group
il suocero, la suocera singly
Covers a spouse's brother and a sister's husband alike
Italian collapses every sibling-in-law into cognato/cognata - and neither doubles as an insult

items.en: nephew, niece, grandson, granddaughter - one word for all four
items.note: Replaces Hindi's whose-sibling split, which Italian has nothing like; the article or the context tells you which relation is meant
abbiamo un bel rapporto; una relazione is usually romantic
i miei = my parents, i tuoi = yours. Very common in speech
Also the address form, used for any adult woman
Shortens to signor before a surname: il signor Rossi
Dated and can grate - use signora for any adult woman
Hindi's behen ji has no Italian counterpart; ragazzi is how you address friends of any gender, well into middle age
Italian's third 'you' isn't an extra intimacy level but the plural; there is nothing below tu
i ragazzi for teenagers and up

items.en: how many children do you have?
items.note: figli = someone's children; bambini = kids in general
con ghiaccio / senza ghiaccio
The 6-to-8pm drink with nibbles thrown in for the price; in Milan a full apericena that replaces dinner. The invitation you're most likely to get.
Stands in for the Hindi list's everyday bread; sold by weight in bakeries
al taglio = by the slice, sold by weight
Plural panini; un tramezzino is the soft triangular one
Always plural in Italian
il minestrone is the thick vegetable one
pasta e ceci is a standard cheap dish
Menus run antipasto, primo, secondo, contorno, dolce

items.en: side dish (the veg with the main)
items.note: A secondo arrives bare - you order the contorno separately
On every restaurant table, usually covered by the coperto
insalata mista = mixed salad
What comes free with an aperitivo; le patatine = crisps
Also a savoury tart: torta salata
una cioccolata (feminine) is the hot drink
Ordered by size: un cono da due gusti
Not to be confused with peperoncino = chilli
The everyday Italian herb, torn over tomatoes and pasta at the last second. Ginger (lo zenzero) barely features in the kitchen.
gli zucchini in the south; okra has no place in Italian food
melanzane alla parmigiana
The Italian everyday herb; coriander (coriandolo) is rare in the kitchen
una spremuta d'arancia = fresh orange juice
Singular in Italian: l'uva è buona
sale e pepe; il peperoncino is the hot one
olio e aceto come to the table with the salad
The everyday tomato base that goes on the pasta. Il ragù is the meat one, la salsa any other sauce.
Offered grated at the table; never on fish
alla spina = on tap; una media is roughly a half-litre, una piccola a third.
Morning only; after a meal it's un caffè, meaning an espresso
The first question at every restaurant table
rosso, bianco; un quarto or mezzo litro della casa. la bibita covers fizzy drinks
acido for something that has gone off
piccante = hot with chilli, and Italian food seldom is
The everyday compliment; squisito is a notch fancier
che gusto vuoi? = which flavour? (ice cream)
prosciutto crudo; pasta should be al dente, not cruda
sono vegetariano / vegetariana; vegano = vegan
cucinare = to cook as an activity; cotto = cooked

items.en: to serve (food); to be of use
items.note: The same verb sits inside mi serve = I need

items.en: dinner's ready, come and sit down
items.note: The call to the table; è pronto! works too

items.en: shall I heat it up for you?

items.note: Restaurants rarely serve it - you'll be sold a bottle
The pressure cooker of the Italian kitchen - every home has one
un barattolo for a jar, una lattina for a can
una camera doppia / singola when booking
il soggiorno is just as common
il tetto = roof; il soffitto = ceiling
Usually plural; al terzo piano senza ascensore
per terra = on the ground or floor; il piano = the storey

items.en: the street door of a building
items.note: You ring the citofono to get through it
hai chiuso a chiave? = did you lock up?
il citofono is the entryphone downstairs
Handy in a hotel: un cuscino in più
Irregular plural of il lenzuolo
Unavoidable in an Italian summer; lo spray antizanzare
Also the national card game
la tazza is the mug-sized one
il dentifricio = toothpaste
buttare la spazzatura; la raccolta differenziata (recycling) is taken seriously
il bidone for the wheelie bin
le pulizie = the cleaning
secco for wine, weather and a dry cough
la lavanderia a gettoni = launderette
Spoken: il caricatore
Pronounced the English way
c'è una presa? - Italy has its own three-pin sockets, so bring an adapter
si è rotto = it's broken
Boilers are small, so it genuinely runs out
The all-purpose complaint: il wifi non funziona, l'ascensore non funziona

items.en: did you turn the gas off?

items.note: Always plural for hair on the head
il viso is the softer, neater word
mal d'orecchie = earache. The plural is irregular and feminine: le orecchie.
mal di denti = toothache; al dente for pasta
mal di schiena = backache
la mente for the mind
respirare = to breathe
Worth having ready for the pharmacy counter
In speech: mi gira la testa
mi dà fastidio = it bothers me
The hurting part is the subject: mi fa male la testa, mi fanno male i piedi
Green cross outside; the pharmacist advises you before a doctor does
Italians blame draughts (il colpo d'aria) for a great deal
sto male = I feel ill; mi fa male = it hurts. Don't mix them up
Formal: dove le fa male?
da + a period covers both 'for' and 'since', with a present-tense verb: ho mal di testa da due giorni
ho vomitato if you actually have been sick
allergica if you're female; essential when ordering
fatta if you're female
Used of pain, colds and moods alike
Formal: si riposi
da + a person = to their place: dal medico, dal dentista
Medicine is 'taken' with prendere, never eaten
Printed on Italian medicine boxes; a digiuno = on an empty stomach
The way to ask at a pharmacy counter
la farmacia di turno is the one open out of hours
quella rossa for a feminine noun
ho caldo = I feel hot; fa caldo = the weather is hot
Never changes: una maglietta rosa, i fiori rosa
Of people and of taste; brutto for ugly or grim
alto for a tall person
Blunt; in polite talk people say in carne
in fretta = in a hurry; forte for strong
Also of a heavy meal or a person who's hard going
a chi lo dai? = who are you giving it to?
entro quando? = by when?
cioè? is the one-word version
ne prendo due = I'll take two of them; ne parliamo dopo. No English equivalent, but unavoidable
a me piace = I like it, with emphasis; plain mi otherwise
After a preposition Italian uses lui and lei, never gli or le
Goes before the verb: lo prendo = I'll take it; non la conosco
gli dico = I'll tell him; le ho scritto = I wrote to her. In speech gli often covers both
un altro = another one; qualcos'altro = something else
non è ancora arrivato = he hasn't arrived yet
The spoken filler: tipo alle otto = like eight-ish

items.en: question words double as relatives: la casa dove abito, il giorno che ci siamo visti
items.note: Hindi's four-way k-/j-/y-/v- grid has no Italian counterpart; one set of words both asks and links, with che as the all-purpose relative
di fronte a = opposite, facing
tra and fra are interchangeable; in mezzo a = in the middle of
verso le otto = around eight
da + a person covers both 'to' and 'at' someone's: vado da Marco, sono dal dentista
più di = more than
The spoken form; altrimenti is the fuller one
non mi piace per niente; assolutamente no is stronger
mi sa che… = I reckon (very spoken)
Does surprise, delight and disbelief; che bello! for pure delight
grazie infinite is warmer still
scusi to anyone you'd address as Lei
senti, scusa with a friend; guardi / guarda opens an explanation
troppo caro = too expensive; it agrees when counting things: troppe persone
tutto il giorno is the everyday way to say 'the whole day'
un sacco di gente; un sacco works alone too: mi piace un sacco
Takes essere in the past: è diventato
devo scappare = I've got to dash
Pulls the subjunctive after it: sembra che sia chiuso
mi preparo in cinque minuti
The standard sign-off on a call or message; ci vediamo = see you

items.en: to come back, to go back
items.note: torno subito = back in a minute

items.en: go and do: andiamo a mangiare, vado a prendere il pane
items.note: The 'a' is compulsory after andare and venire
sta piovendo for right this minute; piove a dirotto = it's pouring
ho una prenotazione a nome … = I've a booking under …
passami Anna = put Anna on
Uber barely exists in Italy; between towns it's the treno or the pullman
Only Rome, Milan, Naples, Turin, Brescia and Catania have one
Stamp it in the machine before boarding or you're fined; also obliterare
Ends in -a but the gender follows the person: un autista / un'autista, like il barista / la barista and il turista / la turista.
lo zaino = rucksack; il sacchetto = carrier bag
Transport strikes are frequent and announced in advance - worth checking before you travel
fare la fila = to queue; in coda = in a tailback
ci vado a piedi = I'll walk there
è qui vicino = it's just nearby
in ritardo = late; in orario = on time

items.en: which platform does it leave from?
items.note: il binario is both the track and the platform

items.en: is this free? (a seat, a table)
items.note: Works for a toilet or a taxi too
The present continuous does duty for the near future here
tenga il resto = keep the change; gli spiccioli are the coins themselves
in contanti = in cash; small bars may still want it
One word for both the card and the machine: posso pagare col bancomat?
Short opening hours - mornings, plus a brief afternoon slot

items.en: what's it going to be? (at a market stall)
items.note: Haggling isn't done in Italian shops; at a market you might get the price rounded down

items.en: can you give me a discount?
items.note: Only plausible at a market or on a big purchase - never in a shop, bar or restaurant
ha da cambiare? - shopkeepers often ask you for exact coins
In speech just il telefono; lo smartphone is also heard
Invariable in the plural: i video
ho il dieci per cento di batteria
non c'è campo = there's no signal; also 'field' and 'pitch'
Feminine, and it elides: un'app, le app.
Said the English way: prenotare online
si è bloccato = it's frozen; non ti sento = I can't hear you
Uses ne for 'about it'
Shortened to l'aria: metti l'aria
Genuinely said, at any age, for good news and bad
che figata! = how cool (young and informal)
The consoling shrug: sono cose che capitano

items.en: not at all; don't mention it
items.note: Answers grazie and waves away any trouble; formal si figuri
ci sta = fair enough (young, spoken)
trovata for a feminine thing
Italian counts mille, diecimila, centomila, un milione - and writes them as one word.

items.en: to greet with a kiss on each cheek
items.note: The Italian greeting ritual with friends and family, left cheek first; men often shake hands instead
il duomo = the main cathedral; shoulders and knees covered to go in
sono arrabbiato = I'm cross
ho paura di volare
cambiare idea = to change your mind
Drops a subject or waves off an offer of help
cantare = to sing
andiamo insieme; Italian has no second word for 'alone' beyond solo / da solo
A whole answer on its own, usually with a shrug; chi lo sa is the fuller version

items.en: can you take me to this address?
items.note: Italian taxis run on the meter by law, so there's no fare to agree first

items.en: ordinals: 1st-10th have their own words, then drop the number's final vowel and add -esimo
items.note: primo, secondo, terzo, quarto, quinto, sesto, settimo, ottavo, nono, decimo, undicesimo…
le sei meno un quarto = quarter to six
al semaforo giri a destra
112 is the single emergency number
possiamo ordinare? = can we order?
giri a destra = turn right; also to wander round a town
quello che voglio = what I want; quello che dici tu
The reply when someone apologises
The resigned shrug at strikes, queues and bureaucracy
posso usare il bagno?
un paio di giorni, un paio di scarpe - the everyday stand-in for 'a couple of'.
Numbers are written as one word: duecentotrentacinque
Said the English way; il fine settimana is the Italian form

items.word: il primo maggio, il due maggio, il quindici agosto
items.roman: il primo maggio, il due maggio, il quindici agosto
items.en: dates: ordinal only for the 1st, plain cardinals after
items.note: Same rule as Hindi. Always with il, and no preposition: parto il tre
Months are lower case; 'in' is a or in: a gennaio
Half the country shuts for it, especially around Ferragosto on the 15th
Standard for a long-term unmarried partner; moglie and marito for spouses
Used loosely for any steady partner, engagement or not
lo sposo, la sposa singly; il matrimonio = the wedding
The respectful word; vecchi is blunt
Fine for things; for people anziano is politer
The service person you'll deal with daily is behind the bar or at your table. Call them with scusi, never a click or a wave.
Irregular plural: le ossa
un amaro is also the after-dinner digestivo
assaggia! = go on, try some - you'll hear it constantly at the table
The Italian shopping unit: due etti di prosciutto, mezzo chilo di pomodori
il forno = the oven
Charged for by law in every shop
Often centrally controlled and switched off by date, not by weather
il boiler is also said
sudare = to sweat

items.en: to get on, to go up
items.note: salire sul treno; the opposite of scendere
Switches to buonasera from mid-afternoon, earlier in the south. Say it on entering any shop or bar
Only when someone is off to bed; buonasera is the evening greeting
Host or friend at the bar; a waiter says cosa prende? or cosa desidera?
The standard opener when you meet or ring after a gap
tranquilla to a woman; non ti preoccupare is the fuller version
Back to front: the missed person is the subject. mi manca l'Italia = I miss Italy
sono impegnato stasera; hai da fare? = are you busy?
sono libero domani; also 'free' as in a vacant seat
The default catch-up question, alongside come va la vita?
sono laureato in storia = I've a degree in history
Italians say università, never 'college': faccio l'università a Bologna
Invariable: le serie
la partita means football unless stated otherwise; forza + team name to cheer
Shortened to il TG (ti-gi); le notizie for news in general
Where you go for anything urgent; il triage sorts you by colour code and 112 is the number to ring.
Plural le ginocchia
tieni! = here, hold this; tenga il resto = keep the change
mi è caduto il telefono = I dropped my phone

items.en: to buy someone a drink, to treat
items.note: ti offro un caffè; offro io = my round. Refusing flat out is a bit rude
Doubles the negative: non c'è nessuno = there's nobody there
Italian guesses with the future: saranno le tre = it must be about three; sarà a casa = he'll be at home

items.en: about to: sto per uscire, stavo per chiamarti
items.note: stare per + infinitive; in the past stavo per = I was just about to
fallo per bene = do it properly
You'll hear it every visit; expect to be pressed twice before a no is taken as real

items.en: let me know when you get there
items.note: fammi sapere on its own = let me know
brava to a woman, bravi to a group - unlike in English, it agrees
che carino! for a child, a gift or a kind gesture
le infradito = flip-flops; also a shape of bread
Buona Pasqua; on Pasquetta, the Monday after, everyone is out of town
la carta d'identità is what Italians carry and what hotels ask for
Italian swallows English nouns whole and wraps them in fare: fare shopping, fare il check-in
sei in vivavoce = you're on speaker
l'onomastico, your name-saint's day, is celebrated too
Always plural; occhiali da sole = sunglasses
Takes over from buongiorno from about 4pm, earlier in the south. Said on walking into any shop or bar, and again on the way out.
Not a pub: it's where you get your coffee standing up, a pastry at 8am and a beer at 7pm. Every other item in this course happens inside one.

items.en: may I come in?; excuse me (squeezing past)
items.note: Said stepping into someone's home, and to get through a crowded bus or lift. The reply from a host is prego, avanti.

items.en: have a good day / a good evening
items.note: The standard exit line from a shop or bar; the reply is grazie, altrettanto. Buonanotte is only for bed.
Cheaper and plainer are la trattoria and l'osteria; a pizzeria only does evenings in many towns.
A per-person charge on nearly every restaurant bill, covering bread and the table. It isn't a service charge and isn't a scam.
Not expected in Italy - the coperto already pays for the table. Rounding up, or a euro or two left on the plate, is plenty.
In many bars you pay at the cassa first and hand the scontrino over at the counter. Keep it: shops can be fined if you leave without one.

items.en: standing at the counter / sitting at a table
items.note: The same coffee costs two or three times more sitting down, and the price list on the wall shows both.
Qui o da portare via? is what you'll be asked at the counter.
The centre of every Italian town and the default meeting point: ci vediamo in piazza, davanti alla chiesa.
Most shut on Mondays. l'ingresso = admission, la mostra = a temporary exhibition.
andiamo al mare is the standard Italian weekend and the whole of August. al mare covers 'at the coast' and 'to the coast'.
Most beaches are paying lidos: un ombrellone e due lettini for the day. La spiaggia libera is the free stretch.
scendo alla prossima = I'm getting off at the next one. Buses stop only if you flag them or press the button.
Un andata e ritorno per Firenze, per favore. One-way is solo andata.
Where you buy bus tickets, stamps and phone top-ups, not just cigarettes. Il tabaccaio is the man behind the counter.
Weigh and label your own fruit before the till. Il forno or la panetteria for bread, l'alimentari for the corner shop.

items.en: to know (a person or a place); to meet for the first time
items.note: conosci Marco? conosco un buon ristorante qui. In the past it means 'met': ho conosciuto Anna a Roma. Sapere is for facts.
esco, esci, esce, usciamo, uscite, escono. usciamo stasera? is how a whole evening gets arranged.
guarda… also opens a sentence, the way English opens with 'look…'. Vedere is to see, guardare is to look on purpose.
credo di sì / credo di no. non ci credo! = I don't believe it.
Opens most opinions: secondo me è troppo caro. Never secondo io - prepositions take me, te, lui.
Rightness is something you have: ho ragione, hai ragione. The opposite is hai torto.
Two jobs. Before a verb it's 'maybe': magari vengo anch'io. As a whole answer, Magari! means 'if only'.
A complete answer on its own. dipende da te = it's up to you.
ti va di uscire stasera? ti va un caffè? The polite version is le va di… Answer volentieri, or magari un'altra volta.
The warm yes to an invitation. mi piacerebbe ma non posso is the soft no.

items.word: mi alzo / ti alzi / si alza
items.roman: mi alzo / ti alzi / si alza
items.en: reflexive verbs: the pronoun goes in front (mi alzo = I get up)
items.note: mi chiamo, mi sveglio, mi vesto, mi riposo, mi diverto. Italian uses far more of these than English, and they all take essere in the past: mi sono alzato.

items.en: impersonal si: 'you / one / people' with a third-person verb
items.note: come si dice? si paga alla cassa. In Italia si cena tardi. A plural thing makes it si mangiano: qui si mangiano bene i dolci.

items.en: how the spelling sounds: c and g soften before e and i, and h hardens them again
items.note: ciao, cena, cinque are ch-; che, chi, chiave are k-. gelato, giro are j-; ghiaccio, spaghetti are hard g. Also gn = ny (gnocchi, bagno), gli = ly (famiglia), sci = sh (sciopero).

items.en: double consonants and stress carry meaning
items.note: Hold the double one: nonno, mamma, caffè, anno. Stress normally lands on the second-to-last syllable; a written accent moves it to the last: città, perché, papà (dad) vs papa (pope).

items.en: questions: same word order, no helper verb, just the tune of the voice
items.note: Italian never inverts and has nothing like 'do you…'. A question word simply goes first: dove abiti? quanto costa? con chi vai?
vorrei, potrei, dovrei and mi piacerebbe are the four you'll use daily to soften a request. Endings: -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero.

items.en: present subjunctive, after penso che, credo che, spero che
items.note: penso che sia chiuso, spero che stia bene, prima che arrivi. Learn sia, abbia, faccia, vada, possa first; you'll hear it constantly even from people who skip it in fast speech.

items.en: two pronouns together: mi + lo becomes me lo, gli/le + lo becomes glielo
items.note: me lo mandi su WhatsApp? te lo dico dopo. The i turns into e: me, te, ce, ve - and gli and le both collapse into glie-.

items.en: Italian city names you have to recognise on a departure board
items.note: Firenze = Florence, Venezia = Venice, Napoli = Naples, Torino = Turin, Genova = Genoa, Milano = Milan, Roma = Rome. The English names are no use to you at the station.
Age is something you have: ho quarantadue anni. Formal: quanti anni ha?
ti presento Marco - and the answer is piacere, with a handshake or two kisses. Formal: le presento mia moglie.
Literally 'into the wolf's mouth'; the reply is crepi, or crepi il lupo. Buona fortuna is thought to bring the opposite.
Italian says 'they have stolen it from me'. At the police station: vorrei fare una denuncia.
i bagagli = luggage; il deposito bagagli = left luggage at a station.
Masculine. c'è l'ascensore? is worth asking before you book a fourth-floor flat, and they are tiny.
che taglia porta? For shoes it's il numero, and posso provarlo? to try it on.
Curious rather than demanding, where a bare perché? can sound blunt: come mai sei qui?
non vedo l'ora di vederti. Literally 'I can't see the hour'.
in primavera, in autunno. With estate and inverno that's the four.
crudo is the cured one, cotto the boiled one. Ordered by the etto at the deli counter: due etti di crudo.
